name: Brazilian / intimate waxing

card.summary: Wax removal of pubic hair, from a swimsuit-line trim to full removal; common and well documented, with ingrown hairs and folliculitis as the usual complaints.
card.aka: Bikini wax, Hollywood wax, intimate waxing
card.note: Pain, ingrown hairs and follicle infections are reported; skin lifting is more likely with certain medications and conditions.

quick.overview:
Brazilian waxing removes most or all pubic hair using warm or cold wax and cloth strips, or stripless hard wax. Related styles include the American (swimsuit-line) and French (landing strip) waxes. The Brazilian name is traced to a Manhattan salon founded in 1987 by seven Brazilian sisters.

It is mainly associated with women but male waxing has become more common. A 2016 JAMA Dermatology survey of 3,316 US women found 84% reported lifetime pubic hair grooming, 59% citing hygiene as the main reason.
quick.mechanism: Wax grips the hair and pulls it out from the follicle, so regrowth typically takes around four to six weeks. Proponents say repeated waxing can weaken regrowth and make sessions less painful and less frequent.
quick.risks: Pain varies from slight to severe. Bumps and ingrown hairs can last two to five days, and folliculitis has been reported to be rising among women who wax or shave the bikini area. People with weakened immune systems face higher infection risk if waxing is done improperly. Critics also raise cultural objections to full removal.

lead: Brazilian waxing, also called intimate or bikini waxing, is the removal of pubic hair with hot or cold wax, lifted off with cloth strips or, in stripless forms, peeled away once hardened.[1][2] People use it to get a smooth, hair-free finish around the bikini line or swimwear area that lasts for weeks rather than days, and some choose it for how clean, sleek or youthful the result looks.[1] Styles range from the American, which removes only the hair a swimsuit would show, through the French, which leaves a narrow vertical strip, to the Brazilian or Hollywood, which removes all or nearly all hair.[1]

Because wax pulls hair out at the root, the skin typically stays bare until regrowth appears, whereas shaving and chemical depilatories cut or dissolve hair at the surface and last hours to days.[6][2] Wikipedia's overview of hair removal lists waxing among the epilation methods whose results last days to weeks, alongside sugaring and threading, with electrolysis and laser as the longer-term options.[6] Proponents also say that repeated waxing leaves regrowth softer and finer, so that sessions become easier over time.[1][2]

The Brazilian name is credited to the J. Sisters salon in Manhattan, opened in 1987 by seven sisters from Brazil.[1] Waxing is mainly associated with women, though male waxing has become more common.[1] Prevalence data come from surveys: a 2016 JAMA Dermatology study of 3,316 American women reported that about 84% had groomed pubic hair at some point, with hygiene the most-cited reason, and a 2017 survey of 7,580 US adults found that 74% groomed, including 66% of men and 84% of women.[1][4][8]

Reported downsides include pain, bumps, ingrown hairs and folliculitis, and survey research has examined associations between grooming and skin infections and injuries.[1][2][8] No clinical trial has tested Brazilian waxing as an intervention; the research base is made up of surveys and descriptive material.[4][7][8]

chain: Wax pulls hair out at the follicle
Skin stays smooth and hair-free for roughly four to six weeks
Clean, sleek bikini-area or body finish
angle.text: Waxing removes hair from the root, so the skin looks smooth and bare for several weeks, longer than shaving. People choose styles from a trimmed swimsuit line to a full Brazilian depending on the look they want.

infobox: 84% of women report lifetime grooming (2016 survey)[4]

paras: In a typical session the area is cleaned with an antiseptic and powdered, wax is applied in the direction of hair growth in strips, and removed against it while the skin is held taut. Long hair may be trimmed first, and a patch test on the upper thigh is commonly recommended to check for allergy.[1] Bikini wax is often a beeswax and tall oil blend, described as stronger on coarse pubic hair than the synthetic waxes used on legs.[1]

Soft or strip wax is spread thinly and removed with a cloth strip, while hard or film wax is applied thicker and peeled off without a strip; hard wax is described as suited to sensitive skin and potentially less painful.[2] Ibuprofen taken beforehand and topical anaesthetics are mentioned as ways to reduce pain, and growth-inhibiting products are sometimes applied afterwards to slow regrowth.[1] Aftercare suggestions in the Wikipedia article include egg oil for the skin.[1]

Waxing can be done by a trained aesthetician in a salon or at home. Wikipedia's article on waxing notes that salon waxing can be costly and that some areas are hard to reach at home, while a licensed aesthetician can cover the whole area in one session.[2]

The American or basic bikini wax removes hair outside a swimsuit triangle and typically takes 20 to 30 minutes. The French wax leaves a landing strip roughly 3.8 cm wide and 7.6 cm long, and is sometimes called a partial Brazilian. The full Brazilian removes hair from the whole area, sometimes leaving a thin strip, and salons use names such as Hollywood or Full Monty.[1] Some people trim without removing anything, and some women trim but leave hair on the outer labia.[1]

Shaving and depilatory creams act at the skin surface, with results lasting hours to days; waxing, sugaring and threading remove hair from the root with results lasting days to weeks; electrolysis, which the article says the US FDA recognises as permanent, and laser hair reduction, FDA-cleared since 1997, are longer-term options.[6] In a 2015 survey of 1,110 US college students, shaving was the most common removal method, used by 82% of women and 49% of men.[7]

Hair removal has been practised in almost every human culture since at least the Neolithic, and has signalled gender roles, status and cleanliness.[6] Pubic hair removal specifically has been recorded in several settings: an ethnologist in 1901 observed it as a custom of Nair women in India, and in Islam removal of unwanted body hair is regarded as part of fitra, or natural practice.[1][9] Wikipedia's pubic hair article describes shaving and waxing becoming more common in the twentieth century as swimsuits shrank, particularly after the bikini's popularisation in the 1940s, and records the designer Rudi Gernreich's 1985 topless 'pubikini' as a counter-example.[5]

The introduction of the bikini in 1946, reduced swimwear coverage and changes in lingerie are all linked in the Wikipedia article to greater interest in grooming.[1] The same article says the practice grew in pornography in the late twentieth century and later spread to women outside it, with waxing becoming common in the late twentieth and twenty-first centuries.[5] Scholars cited there treat total body-hair removal as part of modern femininity.[1]

Some people regard a fully bare result as glamorous or youthful-looking, while others style or skip grooming for identity, religious or cost reasons.[1] Hair removal norms vary by region: the hair-removal article notes that there is less pressure to remove body hair in China and much of Asia, while Middle Eastern societies have long treated regular removal of underarm and pubic hair as proper hygiene.[6]

A 2010 Journal of Sexual Medicine survey of 2,451 US women aged 18 to 68 found that most still had at least some pubic hair, and that total removal was associated with younger age, relationship status and recent oral sex.[7] The 2016 JAMA Dermatology study, a cross-sectional analysis of a nationally representative January 2013 survey, included 3,316 women; 83.8% reported grooming, women aged 45 and older were much less likely to groom than women aged 18 to 24, and women of every racial group groomed less than white women, while income, relationship status and region were not associated with grooming.[4]

Hygiene was the most common reason, cited by 59% according to Wikipedia's summary of that study.[1] Men are surveyed less often: the 2017 STI Journal study put male grooming at 66% in a probability sample of 7,580 US adults, and Wikipedia's pubic hair article cites a 2017 study finding about half of US men groomed regularly.[8][5] In the 2015 student survey, 60% of men said they preferred a hair-free partner compared with 24% of women, and 50% of women described their usual status as hair-free against 19% of men.[7]

Wikipedia notes that male waxing has become more common, citing a 2005 USA Today article on the trend.[1] The hair-removal article describes body-hair depilation among men growing in some Western subcultures, often called manscaping, and recommends trimming before shaving.[6] Published research on men is mostly about how many groom and by what method, not about waxing specifically.[6][7]

Pain ranges from slight to severe, may be greater during pregnancy and may lessen over later sessions.[1] Bumps and ingrown hairs occur, with discomfort typically lasting two to five days; isolated ingrown hairs can be removed with tweezers or electrolysis.[1] Medical providers have reported an increase in folliculitis among women who wax or shave the bikini area, and people with weakened immune systems face a higher infection risk if waxing is done improperly.[1] Wikipedia's pubic hair article adds that Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of grooming-related folliculitis, some cases progress to abscesses, and depilatory wax can burn even when used as directed.[5]

Skin lifting is more likely with blood thinners, steroids, autoimmune drugs, topical retinoids, recent sunburn, laser or peels, and conditions such as eczema or psoriasis. Waxing can also trigger cold sores in people with a history of them.[2]

A 2017 study in Sexually Transmitted Infections analysed a probability sample of 7,580 US adults and found that ever having groomed was associated with self-reported sexually transmitted infections (odds ratio 1.8), with stronger associations for cutaneous infections and for frequent or extreme groomers; the authors noted the cross-sectional design shows association, not causation.[8] Wikipedia reports the same literature alongside a claim that waxing contributed to a decline in pubic lice, and a 2017 study found that about a quarter of groomers had experienced at least one grooming-related injury.[1][5] In the 2015 student survey, 80.3% of those who groomed had experienced genital itching, the most common side effect.[7]

Brazilian waxing is described as the most controversial style.[1] Critics argue it can make adult women look underage and may owe part of its popularity to the sex industry; supporters describe it as a personal grooming and hygiene choice, and the 2016 survey found hygiene to be the most-cited motivation.[1][4] Some people object to any styling on grounds of cost or ideology, and a 2007 news report of a woman with a severe infection after a bikini wax is cited in the Wikipedia article as an example of what can happen if waxing is done improperly.[1]

No studies found testing Brazilian waxing as an intervention. Survey and cohort-type research describes how common pubic hair grooming is and what is associated with it: a 2016 JAMA Dermatology survey of 3,316 US women (83.8% groomed),[4] a 2010 survey of 2,451 women,[7] a 2015 survey of 1,110 college students,[7] and a 2017 probability sample of 7,580 adults linking grooming to self-reported infections.[8] None of these evaluates waxing outcomes directly.

lore.intro: Waxing is discussed less as a looksmaxxing technique than as everyday grooming: it comes up occasionally on T Nation in off-topic banter and in practical exchanges about regrowth, and in wider culture around manscaping and body-hair norms.[3][6]

claims.claim: Waxing at longer intervals does not thin the hair
claims.believers: One T Nation poster said they went every six weeks, then every four, and that spreading sessions out did not thin the hair, advising others to see how fast their own hair regrows first.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's summary of the topic says repeated waxing can weaken hair so it grows more slowly and becomes easier to remove; no clinical trial of this is cited.[1]

claims.claim: A Brazilian wax is the more hygienic way to groom
claims.believers: Many women who groom give hygiene as their main reason; in the 2016 JAMA Dermatology survey summary, 59% cited it.[1][4]
claims.experts: The 2017 Sexually Transmitted Infections study found grooming associated with self-reported infections, and Wikipedia reports a rise in folliculitis among women who wax or shave, though the study design shows association only.[8][1]

claims.claim: Hard wax hurts less than strip wax
claims.believers: Salons and the Wikipedia waxing article describe hard wax as suited to sensitive skin and potentially less painful than strip wax.[2]
claims.experts: The sources describe this as a potential difference and no head-to-head trial is cited; pain is reported to vary from slight to severe and to lessen over later sessions.[1][2]

claims.claim: Waxing leaves skin smooth for weeks, longer than shaving
claims.believers: Proponents point to regrowth taking around four to six weeks, against days for shaving.[6][1]
claims.experts: The hair-removal overview lists waxing results as lasting days to weeks and shaving as hours to days.[6]

claims.claim: Full removal makes adult women look younger or underage
claims.believers: Some people consider a bare result more youthful-looking, and cite this as part of the appeal.[1]
claims.experts: Critics cited in the Wikipedia article argue the same appearance is a reason to object to the Brazilian, and the claim is a cultural one that research has not measured.[1]

claims.claim: Male waxing and manscaping are becoming more common
claims.believers: Wikipedia cites a 2005 USA Today article on growing male waxing, and the hair-removal article describes manscaping as a growing practice in some Western subcultures.[1][6]
claims.experts: Survey data in 2015 and 2017 show men groom widely, with 66% of men grooming in a 2017 sample and shaving the most common method among students.[8][7]

claims.claim: Grooming raises the chance of skin infections or STIs
claims.believers: Some commentators link frequent removal to higher infection risk, and an NPR report cited in Wikipedia's pubic hair article made that link in 2016.[5]
claims.experts: A 2017 probability sample found an association (odds ratio 1.8 overall, higher for frequent groomers) but the authors stress it is cross-sectional and does not show cause.[8]
